features: Foliage forms flat, fanlike sprays of tiny overlapping scales.
Pale butterfly-shaped markings often show on the underside of a spray.
Mature trunks have fibrous, reddish-brown bark in long vertical strips.
lookalikes: Other arborvitae and false cypresses also have scale leaves. Use the underside pattern together with the small, elongated cones rather than the foliage outline alone.
design: Use as an evergreen screen where soil stays reasonably moist and the planting has room to grow.
ecology: Shade-tolerant seedlings can establish in the understory of a coastal forest.
controversy: On hotter, drier campus sites, when is it worth protecting and watering existing redcedars, and where should new plantings use a different species?
tour: At Fairview Grove, UBC’s Beaty addition plan called for retaining 29 trees, primarily cedars and Douglas-firs, and removing 14. Use the grove to ask how a building footprint shapes what survives.

photo.title: Thuja plicata (iNaturalist photo 250896876)
photo.alt: Flattened fans of green foliage have overlapping scale leaves.

features: Hanging seed cones have a three-pronged bract sticking out from beneath each scale.
Needles are single and flat, with two pale bands beneath.
Older trunks show thick, deeply furrowed bark.
lookalikes: Grand fir has upright cones that break apart on the tree. Douglas-fir drops intact cones with protruding bracts.
design: Give a future large canopy ample soil and space, and place paths and infrastructure with the mature tree in mind.
ecology: Douglas-fir can establish after wildfire and persist as a long-lived canopy tree.
controversy: During campus redevelopment, how much building flexibility would you trade to retain a mature Douglas-fir canopy?
tour: Pass around a fallen cone and look for the three points of a bract. Then compare the bark of a young tree and a mature one.

photo.title: Pseudotsuga menziesii (iNaturalist photo 117178182)
photo.alt: Slender, flat needles project from both sides of a woody twig.

features: Opposite, nearly round leaves usually have seven to nine toothed lobes.
Paired winged fruits spread almost straight across from one another.
Often a many-stemmed small tree, with arching or sprawling stems in shade.
lookalikes: Japanese maple often has narrower, more deeply divided lobes. Because cultivars vary, also compare the almost straight-across fruit wings of vine maple.
design: Use as a small understory tree at a woodland edge with room for a spreading, multi-stemmed habit.
ecology: Low stems can root where they touch the ground, allowing vine maple to spread by layering.
controversy: On a narrow path, where can a vine maple keep its natural form, and where does pedestrian clearance call for a different planting?
tour: Musqueam’s plant signs at UBC describe how springy sic̓əɬp stems were used in a fortification near campus. Look for the sign and listen to Elder Larry Grant’s pronunciation.

photo.title: Acer circinatum (iNaturalist photo 376084218)
photo.alt: Broad, rounded green leaves with radiating pointed lobes.

features: Opposite leaves, usually with five broad, pointed lobes.
A freshly broken leaf stalk usually exudes milky sap.
Paired winged fruits spread widely, often nearly in a straight line.
lookalikes: Sugar maple has clear sap in the leaf stalk and its paired fruit wings usually angle closer together. Compare a few mature leaves and fruits where possible.
design: Its dense crown gives street shade. Allow generous rooting space where surface roots could lift paving.
ecology: Fertile trees can produce abundant seedlings that compete with native plants in nearby woodlands.
controversy: Where Norway maple is recruiting into woodland, would you retain a mature shade tree and manage seedlings, or schedule replacement? What would you measure first?
tour: Have the group compare the angle of fallen maple samaras. Then look below an adult tree for seedlings and discuss how far a planting can spread.

photo.title: Acer platanoides (iNaturalist photo 678451031)
photo.alt: A pale broad maple leaf with sharply pointed lobes and shallow gaps.

features: Opposite leaves typically have five to nine sharply pointed, toothed lobes.
The lobes are usually divided deeply toward the base, with wide variation among cultivars.
Slender young twigs can be green or reddish, often on a small multistemmed tree.
lookalikes: Vine maple typically has a rounder leaf outline and broader, shallower lobes. Inspect several leaves because cut-leaf cultivars can blur the distinction.
design: Use as a small specimen in a sheltered courtyard or under a light canopy. Exposed, hot sites can scorch its foliage.
ecology: At Nitobe, the garden staff observed that fallen seeds germinated among mosses, producing seedlings the staff routinely remove.
controversy: When a culturally important planting self-seeds, which seedlings would you keep, share or remove? How would your answer change near a restoration site?
tour: Nitobe Memorial Garden uses Japanese maple and vine maple on opposite sides of a pond that represents the Pacific. Use the pairing to ask what the plants contribute to the design.

photo.title: Acer palmatum (iNaturalist photo 324775188)
photo.alt: Slender pointed lobes radiate from the bases of green leaves.

features: Opposite, palmately lobed leaves. Several cultivars have five deeply cut lobes.
On trees that fruit, paired samara wings may be intermediate in length between red and silver maple.
Cultivar form varies from narrow and upright to broadly oval. Fall colour also varies.
lookalikes: Red and silver maple are its parents. Red maple often has shallower lobes, while silver maple often has deeper sinuses. Shapes overlap, so use paired fruits, a reliable planting record, or leave a field identification tentative.
design: Select a cultivar with a mature crown width that fits the available space. Some cultivars selected for street planting are much narrower than others.
ecology: Red and silver maple hybridize naturally where their ranges overlap in eastern North America. Cultivated selections show different mixtures of parental traits.
controversy: If a cultivar is sold under both red maple and Freeman maple, how should a campus inventory record it? Which evidence would justify a species-level label?
tour: Compare a Freeman maple and its parent species if available. Ask whether leaf shape alone is enough, then explain why a gardener’s label or planting record can be valuable.

photo.title: Acer × freemanii (iNaturalist photo 763250424)
photo.alt: Green, pointed maple leaves with deep gaps between the main lobes.

features: Alternate leaves with long tips and finely bristle-tipped teeth.
Horizontal lenticels make conspicuous dashes across the bark.
Showy spring flower clusters. Petal count, colour and bloom time vary among cultivated forms.
lookalikes: Yoshino cherry often opens pale, mostly five-petalled flowers before the leaves. A dense cluster of double pink blossoms fits cultivars such as ‘Kanzan’. Use flower structure and a cultivar record together.
design: Use as a flowering accent or in a small group where the spring display is easy to see from a path.
ecology: Several cultivated flowering cherries have mixed ancestry. Many are grafted, so shoots from below the graft can belong to a different cherry.
controversy: When replacing a flowering cherry avenue, how much should the design prioritize a synchronized blossom display, and how much should it diversify the planting?
tour: Ask people to compare leaf-out and flower development. UBC Botanical Garden uses cultivar-specific bloom times to guide visitors through its cherry season.

photo.title: Prunus serrulata (iNaturalist photo 1197777)
photo.alt: A tree in spring with a spreading crown full of pale blossoms.

features: Stiff, dark needles in bundles of two, often about 8–12 cm long.
Egg-shaped seed cones, roughly 4–8 cm long, sometimes grouped.
Resinous buds and a crown that often spreads and flattens with age.
lookalikes: Japanese black pine also has paired needles, but often sports conspicuously silvery-white, non-resinous terminal buds. Use the buds and cones alongside needle length.
design: Allow room for the broad mature crown when using it as an evergreen screen. It tolerates a range of soils and some salt exposure.
ecology: Some needles remain on the branch for several years, so a healthy twig often carries multiple years of foliage.
controversy: How should disease susceptibility weigh against salt and drought tolerance when choosing pines for a streetscape? Austrian pine is susceptible to Diplodia shoot blight.
tour: Count the needles in a bundle, then use the bud and cone to test which pine you are seeing. ‘Black pine’ can refer to more than one species.

photo.title: Pinus nigra (iNaturalist photo 166421083)
photo.alt: Long, stiff dark-green needles stand out from a pine twig.

features: Alternate leaves with broad, pointed lobes ending in fine bristles.
Large acorns rest in a shallow, saucer-shaped cup.
The mature tree often has a broad crown with large, rising limbs.
lookalikes: Garry oak has rounded lobe tips. Pin oak also has bristles, but typically has deeper leaf sinuses, smaller acorns and downward-sloping lower branches.
design: Its broad canopy can shade a lawn or plaza edge with ample soil space. Provide drainage and account for acorn drop near paths.
ecology: Acorns take two growing seasons to mature and provide food for wildlife in the tree’s native range.
controversy: For a ceremonial tree, how would you balance visual impact, longevity and support for regional biodiversity? Would the priorities differ beside a restoration site?

photo.title: Quercus rubra (iNaturalist photo 764456084)
photo.alt: Gray trunk bark has long, pale ridges and narrow darker grooves.

features: Small, rounded heart-shaped leaves with finely scalloped edges.
Leaves are often opposite or nearly opposite on the longer shoots.
Senescing foliage can give off a sweet, burnt-sugar scent in autumn.
lookalikes: Eastern redbud also has heart-shaped leaves. Its leaves are alternate and typically have smooth margins. Its flattened pods are much longer than katsura’s small pods.
design: Use as a specimen where autumn scent can be noticed and the root zone can stay moist through dry spells.
ecology: Katsura is typically dioecious. Small pollen and seed-bearing flowers usually occur on different trees.
controversy: Would you specify katsura for its fall colour and scent in a site that needs summer irrigation, or choose a species better suited to that moisture regime?
tour: Ask what can identify a tree without sight. Autumn katsura leaves release a sweet scent associated with maltol. The scent may be faint on an individual leaf.

photo.title: Cercidiphyllum japonicum (iNaturalist photo 649953742)
photo.alt: A drooping branch with round, blunt-toothed green leaves.

features: Opposite leaves with pointed tips and veins curving toward the tip.
Four pointed showy bracts surround the tiny flowers, usually after the leaves emerge.
Round, bumpy pink-to-red fruit hangs from a long stalk.
lookalikes: Pacific dogwood usually has more than four bracts, and its fruit head shows separate small drupes. Kousa’s mature fruit looks like a fused, bumpy sphere. Hybrids can combine traits.
design: Its small stature and layered branching suit a courtyard with well-drained soil and some room for horizontal spread.
ecology: Birds eat the ripe fruit. Each bumpy fruit develops from a group of small flowers.
controversy: When disease has affected native dogwoods at a site, how would you weigh a locally native planting against an introduced or hybrid dogwood selected for landscape performance?
tour: Ask visitors to count the pointed bracts, then look for the tiny flowers at the centre. UBC documented removal of a Pacific dogwood near Ponderosa F after suspected leaf blight, a local lead for discussing tree choice.

photo.title: Cornus kousa (iNaturalist photo 4116663)
photo.alt: Tapered, curved-veined green leaves with white bracts on the same branch.

features: Alternate, usually five-pointed star-shaped leaves with fine teeth.
Hard, prickly spherical fruit clusters often persist into winter.
Some twigs develop raised corky wings.
lookalikes: Maples have opposite leaves and paired winged fruits. Sweetgum staggers its leaves along the twig and carries woody spiky balls.
design: Use for fall colour where there is soil volume for its roots and space for the fruit to fall clear of busy walking surfaces.
ecology: The hard fruit ball opens through small holes and releases many winged seeds.
controversy: Where sweetgum fruit collects on an accessible path, would you move the path, budget for cleanup or choose a low-fruiting selection? What else might you trade away?
tour: Use a fallen fruit to ask how an unmoving wooden ball disperses seeds. Then compare the leaf arrangement with a nearby maple.

photo.title: Liquidambar styraciflua (iNaturalist photo 74204086)
photo.alt: Glossy green leaves with long lobes arranged like a star.

features: Bark flakes off to expose patches of cream, green and grey.
Alternate, maple-shaped leaves are generally broad and three- to five-lobed.
Round seed heads hang on long stalks, frequently in pairs.
lookalikes: American sycamore shares the mottled bark but often has one fruit ball per stalk. A pair favours London plane. Confirm with several fruiting stalks or a planting record.
design: A large street shade tree where there is room for its mature crown. Allow for fallen leaves, twigs and seed heads.
ecology: The round seed heads come apart in winter, releasing small fruits with hairs that help them move in the wind.
controversy: In a long avenue, how would you balance a consistent canopy against diversification for disease resilience? Even within London plane, cultivars vary in anthracnose susceptibility.
tour: Have the group identify the tree from its bark in winter, and then look up for seed heads. It is a hybrid of American sycamore and oriental plane.

photo.title: Platanus × hispanica (iNaturalist photo 759719962)
photo.alt: The trunk surface has patches of gray, tan and pale peeling bark.

features: Short, flat needles of noticeably different lengths grow along the same twig.
Tiny hanging cones are usually about 2 to 2.5 cm long.
The top shoot often bends over, and branch tips tend to droop.
lookalikes: Mountain hemlock typically has bluer needles spreading around the twig and larger cones. Young Douglas-fir has larger cones with three-pronged bracts.
design: Plant as a long-term canopy tree in a sheltered woodland setting with moist rooting soil.
ecology: Seedlings can take root on a decaying log, then extend roots down toward the forest floor.
controversy: Where can a rotting log remain as a nursery for seedlings, and where does heavy foot traffic make a different location more suitable?
tour: Look for a hemlock with exposed roots that straddle an empty space. A now-decayed nurse log is one possible explanation for that shape.

photo.title: Tsuga heterophylla (iNaturalist photo 765367272)
photo.alt: Short, uneven-length needles surround a twig with small brown cones.

features: Small alternate heart-shaped leaves with finely toothed edges.
Look for rusty hair tufts where major veins meet on the leaf underside.
Fragrant early-summer blossoms and later small nutlets hang from a long, strap-like bract.
lookalikes: Largeleaf linden generally has larger leaves and more hairy undersides, with pale hair tufts. Combine underside hairs with fruit characters because leaf size can overlap.
design: Use as a shade tree where its mature crown fits. An avenue can emphasize its upright form and fragrant bloom.
ecology: Nectar-rich flowers attract bees and other pollinators in early summer.
controversy: If aphids drip honeydew onto benches, how would you weigh the value of the tree’s shade and flowers against the maintenance demand? Would relocating seating solve the conflict?

photo.alt: A small pale-green heart-shaped leaf has serrated edges.

features: Opposite leaves are large, with five main lobes and deep cuts between them.
Paired winged fruits have visibly hairy seed bodies.
Older bark becomes ridged and often carries mosses and lichens.
lookalikes: Norway maple usually has shallower cuts between the lobes and smooth seed bodies. Use both leaf shape and fruit hairs when available.
design: Use the spreading crown to shade a spacious lawn or woodland edge where roots and branches can extend.
ecology: Its trunks and larger limbs can support epiphytes such as licorice fern.
controversy: If a mature maple conflicts with a path upgrade, how should the design account for the habitat on its limbs and trunk as well as the shade it provides?

features: Large white bracts, often six, surround a small cluster of true flowers.
Oval leaves are opposite, with conspicuous veins curving towards the tip.
Fruit forms a tight cluster of separate orange to red drupes.
lookalikes: Kousa dogwood usually has four pointed bracts and a single, fused, bumpy fruit. Check fruit or several blooms if a bract count is ambiguous.
design: Use as a small flowering tree in partial shade with well-drained, organic soil. Avoid exposing its bark to intense afternoon sun.

photo.title: Cornus nuttallii (iNaturalist photo 4879338)
photo.alt: Broad, curved-veined leaves near a red cluster of small fruits.

features: Fan-shaped leaves with repeatedly forked veins and often a notch at the outer edge.
Leaves cluster at the tips of short spur shoots.
Deciduous foliage typically turns bright yellow in autumn.
lookalikes: Katsura has a rounded, heart-shaped blade with distinct veins radiating from its base. Ginkgo’s fan has a tapered base and finer veins that repeatedly fork.
design: Used as an urban shade tree on difficult sites. Where fallen seed coverings would create a cleanup burden, designers often specify a pollen-producing cultivar.
ecology: Pollen and seeds usually occur on separate trees. The plum-like structure is the fleshy coat of a gymnosperm seed.
controversy: Should a public planting prioritize the easy maintenance of pollen-producing cultivars, or make room for seed-bearing trees and the opportunity to see their full life cycle?

photo.title: Ginkgo biloba (iNaturalist photo 74219634)
photo.alt: A hand holds a wide green fan-shaped leaf.

features: Leaves are alternate and coarsely toothed, with margins that curl under.
Small woody seed clusters resemble cones and can persist after leaf fall.
Bark is relatively smooth and light grey, often mottled by lichens.
lookalikes: White alder has finer teeth and leaf margins that generally stay flat. The rolled-under edge is a more reliable clue than bark colour.
design: Use as a quick-establishing pioneer in open, moist restoration sites.
ecology: Frankia bacteria in alder root nodules fix nitrogen, increasing nitrogen availability in the surrounding soil over time.
controversy: Would you retain self-seeded alder as early cover after construction or thin it to give planted trees more light?
tour: An alder’s cone-like structures are woody flower clusters. Use one to compare how a flowering tree and nearby conifers package their seeds.

photo.title: Alnus rubra (iNaturalist photo 725378440)
photo.alt: Oval leaves have toothed edges and strong, parallel side veins.

features: Lower branches often carry flat needles spread in two distinct rows.
Needles often have notched tips and two pale bands on the underside.
Cylindrical seed cones stand upright and break apart as they mature.
lookalikes: Douglas-fir cones hang down and fall whole. Western hemlock cones also hang, and they are much smaller.
design: Use as a specimen in a park-scale space with room for a tall conical crown.
ecology: Seedlings can regenerate beneath partial canopy. The provincial compendium reports better survival in moderate shade than in the open.
controversy: A young grand fir fits a small space. How much room should a campus planting plan reserve for its mature crown, and what would that space displace?

photo.title: Abies grandis (iNaturalist photo 177381488)
photo.alt: Flat, shiny needles spread out in two ranks along a twig.

features: Flat, soft needles sit in opposite pairs along short shoots.
The foliage turns rusty in autumn and drops, leaving the crown bare in winter.
Reddish-brown trunk bark fissures and peels in strips as the tree matures.
lookalikes: Bald cypress also loses its foliage but has alternate needles along its shoots. Coast redwood keeps live green foliage through winter and its flat needles are arranged alternately.
design: Use as a large specimen on an open site with moist, well-drained soil and room for its tall crown.
ecology: Pollen and seed cones develop on the same tree. The genus has a fossil history in western North America, while the living species is native to China.
controversy: When a lineage is known from regional fossils, what time scale should guide use of the word ‘native’ in a campus planting plan?

Shiny, leathery oval leaves stay on the tree through winter.

Open-grown mature trees often develop a broad crown with heavy, crooked limbs.

photo.title: Quercus garryana (iNaturalist photo 671444517)

features: Many side shoots carry flat needles in two apparent ranks, with pale bands below.
Bark is reddish-brown and fibrous. The crown retains green foliage through winter.
Relatively small, egg-shaped seed cones, generally around 2 cm long.
lookalikes: Dawn redwood has paired opposite needles and loses its leaves in winter. Giant sequoia has overlapping awl-like foliage on rounded shoots and substantially larger cones.

Mature bark is very thick, soft-fibrous and deeply furrowed.
Woody, egg-shaped seed cones are commonly about 5–9 cm long.

photo.title: Sequoiadendron giganteum (iNaturalist photo 748103901)
photo.alt: A massive orange-brown trunk flares broadly near the ground.

features: Stiff, sharply pointed needles are green above and silvery beneath.
Needles attach to short woody pegs that stay on an older bare twig.
Thin grey or purplish-brown bark breaks into small scaly plates.
lookalikes: Blue forms of Colorado spruce often look silvery on both sides of the needle. Sitka spruce usually has a stronger contrast between upper and lower surfaces.
design: Use as a large specimen where the soil stays moist and the sharp foliage can sit clear of pedestrian routes.
ecology: Sitka spruce tolerates coastal salt spray and can grow on soils influenced by brackish water.
controversy: Would you plant Sitka spruce on an exposed site because it tolerates salt spray, if you expect the soil itself to become drier?
tour: Turn over a low branchlet to see its two-toned needles. Use the tree to ask why tolerance of coastal spray and tolerance of dry soil are different traits.
